intro: How I design a site, from the first conversation to launch and back into the kit. Each step answers one question, says which skill or tool helps, and what I should have when it's done. Skip steps on small sites, but don't change the order: deciding what goes on the page comes before how it looks, and how it looks comes before how it moves.

steps.title: Brief
steps.question: What is this site, who is it for, and what should a visitor do or feel?
steps.why: Every later decision gets checked against the brief. Without one, the design follows whatever I saw last on a gallery.
do: Write down what the site is, who it's for, and the one thing a visitor should do or feel
List the content that really exists: how many projects or products, photos, video, how much copy
Note the tone in a few words, plus sites or things outside the web it should feel like
Write the must-haves and the no-gos, and the limits (paid fonts, WebGL, who edits it later)

tools.label: site-concept
tools.note: step 1 asks these questions and writes the brief back

done: Someone else could read the brief and explain the site
The content list has real numbers

steps.title: Research
steps.question: What have others done, and what do I already love that fits?
steps.why: Designers don't start from a blank page. They look at a lot of work and pick out ideas worth learning from: a principle, not a feature list.
do: Go through my pins first: what fits this brief, and what would it become here?
Look for what the pins don't cover on the galleries (minimal.gallery first) and ABC Dinamo
Save good finds as pins, each with what to look at and why
Respect the nope pins: they are lessons

tools.label: add-to-kit
tools.note: turns a site into pins (and maybe a theme or blocks)

tools.label: site-concept
tools.note: step 2 walks every pin against the brief

steps.output: Pins for the project, and a research list of threads worth pulling
done: Every thread is backed by pins or a gallery site
I can say why each one fits this brief

steps.title: Concept
steps.question: What is the one idea this site is built on?
steps.why: The concept is what makes the site feel designed instead of assembled. It settles later questions for me: does this help the idea or not?
do: Look at 2–3 concepts that differ in the idea itself, not in three palettes on one layout
Pick one (or mix), and prototype its signature moment before anything else
Turn it into a written plan: idea, principles, visual system, pages, motion, kit map

tools.label: site-concept
tools.note: concepts on a board, the signature prototype, then CONCEPT.md

steps.output: concept/CONCEPT.md, the board and the signature prototype
done: The idea fits in one sentence
The signature moment works in a real browser
Every kit piece has a 'from → to'

steps.title: Content and structure
steps.question: Which pages are there, what's on each, and in what order?
steps.why: This is the step beginners skip. Deciding what goes on the page before how it looks prevents layouts that don't fit the real copy, and it usually makes the site simpler.
do: Write the sitemap: every page, and how people move between them
For each page, list the sections in order, with what each one has to say or show
Write the real copy (or a close draft) for every section, at its real length
Make the asset list: every image, video and file, what exists and what's missing

tools.label: site-layout
tools.note: part 1 writes concept/CONTENT.md with the sitemap, sections, copy and assets

steps.output: concept/CONTENT.md: sitemap, sections, copy and asset list
done: No section is just 'some text here'
The asset list says who supplies what

steps.title: Visual system
steps.question: Which type, colours, spacing and grid does every page share?
steps.why: A small system of type sizes, colour roles, a spacing scale and a grid is what makes a site feel consistent. Deciding it once means I don't decide it again on every page.
do: Start from the concept's theme.json, or from a kit theme
Try the type scale on the real copy: the longest heading, the bio, a caption
Check every text colour against its background
Pick the grid (columns, gutter, margin) and how it changes on the phone

tools.label: site-layout
tools.note: part 2 builds a specimen page to tune the system on the real copy

steps.output: concept/theme.json, and the specimen page in concept/system/
done: Five type sizes or fewer, all tested on real copy
Every text colour passes contrast
The grid is written down with numbers

steps.title: Layout
steps.question: How does each section sit on the grid, on a big screen and on a phone?
steps.why: Grey boxes first, so I judge the arrangement and not the colours. Two or three options per key section, compared side by side, beat polishing the first idea.
do: Wireframe each page as grey boxes on the grid, with the real copy
Make 2–3 options for the sections that matter (hero, work, project page)
Look at every option at phone and desktop width, then pick
Switch the chosen wireframes to the visual system to check the styled version

tools.label: site-layout
tools.note: part 3 builds switchable wireframes with phone and desktop views

tools.label: Figma
tools.note: optional, when a page is easier to compose by hand

steps.output: concept/wireframes/ and the chosen options in concept/LAYOUT.md
done: Every page has a chosen layout at both widths
The squint test passes on every page

steps.title: Motion and interaction
steps.question: What moves, when, and what does each movement tell the visitor?
steps.why: Motion comes after layout so it serves a page that already works. The signature moment is already proven; this step gives the rest of the site one calm motion language.
do: Write the motion language: easings, durations, what scroll, hover and page changes do
Prototype anything risky as a small HTML page or a study before building it into the site
Design the touch version and the reduced-motion version of every interaction

tools.label: pnpm kit study <slug> --p5
tools.note: a new study, in GSAP or p5.js

steps.output: The motion section of CONCEPT.md, plus prototypes for anything new
done: Every animation has a job
Touch and reduced-motion versions exist

steps.title: Build
steps.question: How do I turn the plan into a real site?
steps.why: Build in the same order as the design: structure, then system, then motion. The site stays usable at every step, and problems show up early.
do: Scaffold from the kit with the concept's theme and blocks
Build every page with real content and plain styling first
Port the signature moment from the prototype, then the other motion
Check the phone version as you go, not at the end
Rework every kit block as the kit map says, never leave it as it came
steps.output: A running site that follows CONCEPT.md and LAYOUT.md
done: Every page works on a phone
No kit block is used unchanged

steps.title: Critique
steps.question: What isn't working yet, and what should I fix first?
steps.why: Designers get their work looked at all the time. A review against the concept's principles and the basics finds the things I've stopped seeing, and explains why they matter.
do: Run a design review after each big change, not only at the end
Fix the top notes first; ignore small things until the big ones are right
Turn anything I learn into an idea or decision pin

tools.label: design-review
tools.note: screenshots at three widths, automatic checks and prioritised notes

done: No 'fix first' notes left
The copy test passes for every kit piece

steps.title: Launch
steps.question: Is it ready for real people, on real devices?
steps.why: The last 10% is what makes a site feel finished: the preview when someone shares the link, the tab icon, a 404 page, speed, and the details people only notice when they're missing.
do: Run the review in launch mode
Go through the checklist below on a real phone too
Deploy, then open the live site and share the link with yourself

tools.label: design-review
tools.note: launch mode checks meta, preview image, favicon, 404 and weight

checklist: Page title and description on every page
Preview image (og:image, 1200×630) and title for shared links
A 404 page in the site's style
Every image has alt text; decorative ones have empty alt
Images exported at the right size (no 4000px photos shown at 600px) and in WebP or AVIF
Fonts licensed for the web (Dinamo trials are only for mockups)
Works with reduced motion, with the keyboard, and on a real phone
No console errors, nothing loads from localhost
Analytics, if wanted, and the domain set up
done: Every checklist item is ticked
The link preview looks right in a chat app

steps.title: Look back
steps.question: What did this site teach me, and what goes back into the kit?
steps.why: This is how the kit becomes mine. Every site should leave behind its own theme, its reworked blocks and its lessons, so the next one starts further ahead.
do: Add the site's theme to the kit under a material name
Bring reworked blocks back as new blocks (or new versions), with usedIn set to the project
Write decision pins for the big choices and idea pins for the lessons
Turn experiments that didn't make it into studies
Note which steps of this process helped and which I'd change

tools.label: add-to-kit
tools.note: for new blocks and themes from the finished site

steps.output: New theme, blocks, pins and studies in the kit
done: The project is in content/projects.json with its pins
At least one kit piece is now my own version
